newsitem.title: USA: GM, UAW settle Oklahoma strike.
newsitem.headline: GM, UAW settle Oklahoma strike.

text.p: General Motors Corp. and the United Auto Workers reached a tentative accord to settle a costly seven-week strike at the company's Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, car plant, a company spokesman said Sunday.
GM spokesman James Farmer said the agreement was reached late Saturday night with bargainers from UAW Local 1999. A ratification vote by the 3,500 striking workers was scheduled for Sunday, he said.
If workers approve the pact, GM hopes to resume production of Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass sedans Tuesday, he said.
"We will be calling some key people back and hopefully will start first-shift production Tuesday," he said.
Farmer would not comment on the terms, which were not released. Union officials speaking anonymously said most of their demands were satisfied.

UAW members struck the plant at midnight April 4 when the two sides could not reach an agreement on a new local contract. The key sticking points were jobs, and other health and safety demands. The union had wanted GM to add 500 jobs to help restore positions lost to retirements and cut down on overtime.
GM, the world's largest automaker, has said it does not need as many workers to produce the new versions of the Malibu and Cutlass, and needs to keep its staffing levels competitive.
GM Chairman Jack Smith and North American Operations President Richard Wagoner gave no hint a settlement was near at the company's annual shareholder meeting in Wilmington, Delaware, on Friday.
In written remarks, Smith said he wished the company could avoid the strikes. But he stressed the company's longstanding position it cannot make settlments that are costly in the long term.

GM said the Oklahoma City strike and a second, still unresolved, dispute at its Pontiac East, Pontiac, Michigan, pickup truck plant have cost it $225 million in lost profits this year as of May 15. For all of 1996, GM lost $1.2 billion in profits because of labor strikes.

Wagoner said Friday the Oklahoma City strike went on much longer than the company and the UAW had anticipated. The strike proved painful for GM because it choked off supplies of the new Malibu just as the automaker was gearing up to take back market share in the key mid-size car segment.

As the strike wore on, GM scaled back its national advertising for the car, which has generally received positive reviews from the automotive press. GM's plant in Wilmington also makes Malibus, but is further behind on its launch curve.

Separately, about 8,500 workers of the International Union of Electronic Workers in Warren, Ohio, approved a new contract settlement on Saturday by a 79 percent margin. Members of IUE Local 717 had staged a one-day strike earlier this month that could have disrupted GM's North American vehicle production.

The agreement guarantees all of the current 8,500 jobs, as well as promises new GM investment at IUE-staffed Ohio parts plants. The IUE workers make electrical components at several plants in the Warren area.
